questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: Which act carries no moral accountability because the will is absent?
questions.rationale: Acts of persons asleep or hypnotized, reflex actions and acts under serious physical violence are not moral acts; the will has no part.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Human acts (PDF p. 11)
questions.quote: Reflex actions where the will has no time to intervene.

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: For an act to be a human act, it must be:
questions.rationale: Human acts are voluntary, not coerced, done with full knowledge and directed toward an end.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Codes as reference points (PDF p. 15)
questions.quote: they must be voluntary, not coerced, done with full knowledge and based on an intention

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A nurse knows the right action but hospital rules prevent her from doing it. She is experiencing:
questions.rationale: Jameton described moral distress as knowing the right thing to do while institutional constraints make it impossible.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Moral distress (PDF p. 11)
questions.quote: knows the right way for performing something but organizational limits would make the execution impossible

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A nurse must choose between two options that both seem good for the patient. This is a(n):
questions.rationale: A dilemma arises when two opposing options appear equally beneficial and only one can be chosen.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Ethical dilemma (PDF p. 11)
questions.quote: whenever we encounter two opposing yet equally beneficial for the patients

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: In Rest's Four Component Model, which comes first?
questions.rationale: Rest's sequence: sensitivity (recognizing the problem), judgment, motivation, then character.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 James Rest's model (PDF p. 16)
questions.quote: (1) moral sensitivity (recognition); (2) moral judgment or reasoning; (3) moral motivation; and (4) moral character

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: A nurse keeps advocating for her patient despite pressure and fatigue. Which Rest component does this show?
questions.rationale: Moral character is persisting in the moral task despite opposition, fatigue and distractions.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 James Rest's model (PDF p. 16)
questions.quote: they must persist in a moral task or action despite obstacles

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: A nurse chooses advocacy over her own job security. Which Rest component is at work?
questions.rationale: Moral motivation means moral values take precedence over competing values like job security or acceptance.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 James Rest's model (PDF p. 16)
questions.quote: Ethical behavior will only result if moral con- siderations take precedence over competing priorities.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Taking bitter medicine to regain health is an example of which kind of good?
questions.rationale: A useful good is desired as a means to another good, like bitter medicine or painful surgery for health.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Moral good (PDF p. 13)
questions.quote: Example: bitter medicine to obtain health or a painful surgery

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Health and virtue, desired for their own sake, are examples of:
questions.rationale: An honorable good is desired in itself for its intrinsic goodness, e.g., virtue and health.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Moral good (PDF p. 13)
questions.quote: Honorable good — is a good which is desired in itself because of its intrinsic goodness

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: The primary precept of natural law is:
questions.rationale: Natural law's first precept is that good is to be done and pursued and evil avoided (beneficence and non-maleficence).
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Natural law (PDF p. 14)
questions.quote: The primary precept of the Natural Law is for Good to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: Which reference point for human acts changes with the time and place of a culture?
questions.rationale: Cultural norms reflect living conditions at a particular time and place, so they keep changing.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Cultural norms (PDF p. 15)
questions.quote: cultural norms are ever changing depending on the cultural conditions surrounding it

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: How does a code of ethics differ from a nursing practice act?
options: A code sets moral ideals; the act is law
A code is law; the act is optional
questions.rationale: A code delineates moral ideals and accountability; the nursing practice act is the law nurses must follow.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Practice acts vs. code (PDF p. 17)
questions.quote: nursing practice acts refer to the laws that govern the nursing profession

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which issuance is the Code of Ethics for Filipino Registered Nurses?
questions.rationale: The Code of Ethics for Nurses was promulgated as Board of Nursing Resolution No. 220, series of 2004.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Nursing code of ethics (PDF p. 17)
questions.quote: The "Code of Ethics for Nurses" BON Resolution 220 series 2004

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: The ICN Code of Ethics names the nurse's fundamental responsibilities as promoting health, preventing illness, restoring health and:
questions.rationale: The four fundamental responsibilities are to promote health, prevent illness, restore health and alleviate suffering.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 ICN Code (PDF p. 17)
questions.quote: 4. to alleviate suffering

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Who first used the term 'bioethics' (1970–1971)?
questions.rationale: Oncologist Van Rensselaer Potter coined bioethics as joining biological knowledge and human values.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 What is bioethics (PDF p. 24)
questions.quote: Van Renssealaer Potter used the term bioethics for the first time in 1971

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: Which document (1947) condemned human experiments without consent after the Nazi trials?
questions.rationale: The Nuremberg Code (1947) required voluntary consent of human subjects.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Recent sources of bioethics (PDF p. 28)
questions.quote: Nuremberg Code (1947) condemned all experimentation on human subjects without their consent.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: The Belmont Report (1979) set three principles of research ethics. Which is one of them?
questions.rationale: Belmont: respect for persons, beneficence and justice, with emphasis on informed consent.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Recent historical landmarks (PDF p. 28)
questions.quote: Respect for persons, Beneficence, Justice

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Black men with syphilis were left untreated even after penicillin was available. This study was:
questions.rationale: The US Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment and is a key reason for research ethics rules.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Abuses in human experimentation (PDF p. 24)
questions.quote: WHO WERE NOT TREATED DESPITE THE DISCOVERY OF PENICILLIN

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Disabled children at Willowbrook were deliberately infected with which virus?
questions.rationale: At Willowbrook State Hospital, children were inoculated with hepatitis virus, with consent coerced from parents.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Recent sources of bioethics (PDF p. 28)
questions.quote: injecting hepatitis virus injected on handicapped children with consent coerced from parents

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which ancient source gave medicine the principle 'first, do no harm'?
questions.rationale: The Hippocratic writings are a remote source of bioethics: do no harm, with paternalism.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Remote sources of bioethics (PDF p. 27)
questions.quote: Hippocratic Oath — "first do no harm"

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: Applying ethical principles to a specific patient case at the bedside is called:
questions.rationale: Clinical bioethics applies theories and principles to concrete clinical cases to guide action.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Subdivisions of bioethics (PDF p. 27)
questions.quote: Clinical Bioethics: Application of ethical theories and accepted general principles to concrete clinical cases

questions.subject: NP II
questions.stem: Early nursing ethics (1880s–1960s) was mainly based on:
questions.rationale: Early nursing ethics was virtue-, relationship- and vocation-oriented, a preventive ethics, not problem-oriented.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 1 Historical perspectives (PDF p. 19)
questions.quote: it is virtue-oriented, relationally- oriented, and call or vocation-oriented
